entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jean I, Duke of Alençon (1385–1415), known as 'the Wise,' was a prominent French nobleman and military commander whose life and death epitomized the tumultuous Hundred Years' War. As a peer of France and a member of a cadet branch of the House of Valois, he held significant feudal power and played a crucial role in the Armagnac-Burgundian civil war, a devastating internal conflict that weakened France even as it faced renewed English aggression. His strategic importance lay in commanding substantial forces and his close ties to the French royal family, positioning him at the heart of the kingdom's defense against Henry V of England.

Born in 1385, Jean I inherited the Duchy of Alençon and the County of Perche in 1404. He distinguished himself early in his military career, notably participating in the siege of Calais in 1406 and later serving under King Charles VI. His involvement in the Armagnac-Burgundian conflict saw him align with the Armagnac faction, opposing John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy. This internal strife culminated in the assassination of Louis I, Duke of Orléans, and further fragmented French political and military unity. Jean I's primary historical moment arrived on October 25, 1415, at the Battle of Agincourt, where he commanded the second division of the French army. Despite a valiant charge that broke through the English lines and reportedly saw him fight within yards of King Henry V, he was ultimately overwhelmed and killed on the field.
